title: Registry, scheduled tasks and execution policy
summary: The registry as a PowerShell drive, scheduled tasks that run pwsh scripts correctly, what execution policy is (and is not), and living with Windows PowerShell 5.1 modules from PowerShell 7.

steps.title: Windows only: the registry is a drive
body: > **Windows only.** Everything on this card needs Windows; writing under `HKLM:` also needs an elevated session.
PowerShell exposes the registry through **providers**, so it behaves like a file system: keys are folders, values
are *properties* of a key.
```powershell
Get-ChildItem HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall      # installed software (64-bit)
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager' -Name PendingFileRenameOperations
Get-ItemPropertyValue HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Contoso\Agent -Name Version               # just the value
New-Item HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Contoso\Agent -Force | Out-Null                          # create the key (and parents)
New-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Contoso\Agent -Name Enabled -PropertyType DWord -Value 1 -Force
Set-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Contoso\Agent -Name Enabled -Value 0
Remove-ItemProperty HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Contoso\Agent -Name Legacy -WhatIf
- `HKLM:` and `HKCU:` are built in; `HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT` and others are reached as `Registry::HKEY_CLASSES_ROOT`.
- `-PropertyType` matters: `DWord` (32-bit number), `QWord`, `String`, `ExpandString`, `MultiString`, `Binary`.
Many settings are only read as a DWord; a string `"1"` silently does nothing.
- 32-bit programs on 64-bit Windows read `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\WOW6432Node\...`: check both when looking for software.
- Export a key before changing it: `reg.exe export HKLM\SOFTWARE\Contoso\Agent agent-backup.reg`.

steps.prompt: Turn on a setting that the agent reads as a 32-bit number, creating the key if needed. (Windows, elevated.)
steps.explain: `New-Item -Force` creates missing parent keys and does not fail if the key exists. The property type names are the registry's own (`DWord`), not .NET's (`Int32`).

steps.title: Windows only: scheduled tasks that run PowerShell
body: The `ScheduledTasks` module builds a task from parts, then registers it:
```powershell
$action    = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'pwsh.exe' -Argument '-NoProfile -NonInteractive -File "C:\Ops Scripts\Clean-Logs.ps1"'
$trigger   = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -Daily -At '02:00'
$principal = New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId 'NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM' -LogonType ServiceAccount -RunLevel Highest
$settings  = New-ScheduledTaskSettingsSet -ExecutionTimeLimit (New-TimeSpan -Hours 2) -StartWhenAvailable
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'Nightly cleanup' -TaskPath '\Ops\' -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -Principal $principal -Settings $settings
What goes wrong in real life, and the fix:
- **`powershell.exe` instead of `pwsh.exe`**: the task runs Windows PowerShell 5.1, and a 7-only script fails.
- **No quotes around a path with spaces** in `-Argument`: `-File C:\Ops Scripts\...` becomes two arguments.
- **No `-NoProfile -NonInteractive`**: a profile changes behaviour, or a `Read-Host` waits forever.
- **A stored user password** that expires: run as `SYSTEM`, a gMSA (group managed service account) or
`-LogonType S4U` instead.
- **No time limit**: a hung run blocks every later run (the default limit is 3 days).
`Get-ScheduledTaskInfo` shows `LastRunTime` and `LastTaskResult`: `0` is success, `1` means the script exited 1,
`267009` (0x41301) still running, `267011` (0x41303) has not run yet, `2147942402` (0x80070002) file not found.

steps.title: Execution policy, and 5.1 modules from PowerShell 7
body: **Execution policy** decides which scripts PowerShell on Windows will run. It is a **safety net against accidents,
not a security boundary**: anyone can run `pwsh -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File x.ps1` or paste the code.
| Policy | Runs |
| `Restricted` | no scripts (Windows PowerShell's default on Windows client editions) |
| `RemoteSigned` | local scripts; downloaded ones only if signed (default on Windows Server, and for PowerShell 7 on Windows) |
| `AllSigned` | only signed scripts |
| `Bypass` | everything, no warnings (for automation that controls its own inputs) |
"Downloaded" means the file carries the **Mark of the Web** (a `Zone.Identifier` alternate data stream added by
browsers and mail clients). If you trust a downloaded script, `Unblock-File .\script.ps1` removes the mark. Set the
policy per user (`Set-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned -Scope CurrentUser`) or by Group Policy, not machine-wide by
hand. On Linux and macOS, execution policy is not enforced.
**Windows PowerShell modules from PowerShell 7.** Most Windows modules (ActiveDirectory, DnsServer, Hyper-V...) work
in 7 directly. For the few that do not, `Import-Module <name> -UseWindowsPowerShell` loads them in a hidden 5.1
process and proxies the commands; results come back deserialised (properties, no methods), like remoting.

steps.prompt: A colleague downloads `Fix-Printers.ps1` from the team wiki and gets *... cannot be loaded. The file is not digitally signed* on a machine with `RemoteSigned`. They read the script and trust it. What is the right fix?
steps.explain: The file has the Mark of the Web, so RemoteSigned asks for a signature. Removing the mark from this one, reviewed file is the narrow fix. Loosening the machine-wide policy changes it for every script, forever.

steps.prompt: Windows PowerShell 5.1 only, or available in PowerShell 7 on Windows?
steps.explain: PowerShell 7 dropped the old DCOM and classic-event-log cmdlets. Their replacements work in both, so a script using `Get-CimInstance` and `Get-WinEvent` runs anywhere on Windows.
